data.label: Corn (field)
data.notes: Hybrids are rated by these degree days from planting to black layer (physiological maturity).

citations.text: Gilmore, E. C. and Rogers, J. S. (1958). Heat units as a method of measuring maturity in corn. Agronomy Journal 50, 611–615.
Neild, R. E. and Newman, J. E. (1987). Growing season characteristics and requirements in the Corn Belt. National Corn Handbook NCH-40, Purdue University.

freeze.note: Kills the whole plant; 32 °F kills leaves.

citations.text: NDSU Extension: Fall frost damage to field crops.

data.label: Soybean
data.notes: The corn setting, as NDAWN and HPRCC's CliGrow use it. Soybean development depends on day length as well as heat, so degree days predict its stages less well than corn's; our soybean stage model uses both.

citations.text: NDAWN (North Dakota Agricultural Weather Network): Soybean growing degree days.

freeze.note: Kills the plant; 28–32 °F damages leaves and pods.

citations.text: NDSU Extension: Fall frost damage to field crops.

data.label: Alfalfa
data.notes: Counted from January 1 in spring, or from the last cutting. HPRCC's CliGrow uses an upper threshold of 77 °F; we use 86 °F, as UW–Madison's alfalfa cutting tool does.

citations.text: Newell, S. Managing fall alfalfa cutting for persistence. UW–Madison Extension Crops and Soils.

freeze.note: A killing freeze, which ends the stand's fall growth.

citations.text: University of Minnesota Extension: Managing alfalfa winter injury.

data.label: Spring wheat
data.notes: North Dakota's method also limits the maximum to 70 °F until the second leaf (Haun stage 2.0), which a single setting can't express; the wheat stage model applies it. HPRCC's CliGrow uses 32/77 °F.

citations.text: Bauer, A., Fanning, C., Enz, J. W. and Eberlein, C. V. (1984). Use of growing-degree days to determine spring wheat growth stages. North Dakota Cooperative Extension Service EB-37.
NDAWN (North Dakota Agricultural Weather Network): Wheat growing degree days.

data.label: Barley
data.notes: As for spring wheat, North Dakota's method also limits the maximum to 70 °F until the second leaf (Haun stage 2.0), which a single setting can't express.

citations.text: NDAWN (North Dakota Agricultural Weather Network): Barley growing degree days.

data.label: Dry (edible) bean
data.notes: HPRCC's CliGrow setting. We found no recent extension publication that sets a base and upper threshold for dry beans; Nebraska gives 1550–1700 degree days from emergence to maturity.

citations.text: HPRCC (High Plains Regional Climate Center): CliGrow.
University of Nebraska–Lincoln CropWatch: Dry beans (August 21, 2009).

freeze.note: Pinto and navy beans are very sensitive to frost: 30–32 °F kills them.

citations.text: NDSU Extension: Fall frost damage to field crops.

data.label: Grain sorghum
data.notes: Black layer (physiological maturity) comes at about 2,700 degree days for short-season hybrids and 3,400 for full-season ones. HPRCC's CliGrow uses an upper threshold of 86 °F.

citations.text: Kelley, J. (2011). Grain sorghum growth and development. In Grain Sorghum Production Handbook, University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service MP297.
Kansas State University Research and Extension: Grain sorghum production handbook, MF-2234.

data.label: Sugarbeet
data.notes: North Dakota's setting, from Holen and Dexter (1997), who found a 34 °F base predicted leaf stages best. HPRCC's CliGrow uses 50/86 °F.

citations.text: Holen, C. D. and Dexter, A. G. (1997). A growing degree day equation for early sugarbeet leaf stages. Sugarbeet Research and Extension Reports 27, 152–157.
NDAWN (North Dakota Agricultural Weather Network): Sugarbeet growing degree days.

data.label: Sunflower
data.notes: North Dakota's setting: temperatures below 44 °F count as 44, with no upper threshold. Physiological maturity (R9) comes at about 2,310 degree days. HPRCC's CliGrow uses 50/99 °F with the same maturity total.

citations.text: Kandel, H. et al. (2020). Sunflower production guide. NDSU Extension A1995.
Schneiter, A. A. and Miller, J. F. (1981). Description of sunflower growth stages. Crop Science 21, 901–903.

freeze.note: Causes little damage once seeds have filled; 28–30 °F injures buds and flowers.

citations.text: Kandel, H. et al. (2020). Sunflower production guide. NDSU Extension A1995.

data.label: Potato (to emergence)
data.notes: Degree days above 4 °C (39.2 °F) from planting, fitted to Wisconsin's emergence dates; 50% emergence comes at about 374 °F·d (208 °C·d). HPRCC's CliGrow uses 45 °F with an upper threshold of 97 °F.

citations.text: UW Vegetable Pathology, Vegetable Crop Updates (2020–2026): planting and 50% emergence dates by location.

data.label: Sweet corn (processing)
data.notes: The field corn setting, used for processing sweet corn. Oregon State uses 44/86 °F for fresh-market varieties.

citations.text: Andrews, N. et al. Vegetable degree-day models: an introduction for farmers and gardeners. Oregon State University Extension EM 9305.

data.label: Green pea (processing)
data.notes: The heat units long used to schedule canning peas. Quebec's processors use 41 °F (5 °C).

citations.text: Katz, Y. H. (1952). The relationship between heat unit accumulation and the planting and harvesting of canning peas. Agronomy Journal 44, 74–78.
Bourgeois, G., Jenni, S., Laurence, H. and Tremblay, N. (2000). Improving the prediction of processing pea maturity based on the growing-degree day approach. HortScience 35, 611–614.

data.label: Snap bean
data.notes: Oregon State's Croptime setting, fitted in western Oregon (2013–2015); we found none fitted in the Upper Midwest. Its authors note that days from planting can predict harvest about as well.

citations.text: Oregon State University Croptime: Bean (snap bean) varieties models, version 1.0 (2020).

data.label: Alfalfa weevil
data.notes: Times alfalfa weevil egg hatch, larval feeding, pupation and new adults from degree days since January 1 (base 48 °F), on NEWA's model, and marks when to scout stem tips for feeding on the first crop.

citations.text: NEWA, Network for Environment and Weather Applications, Cornell University: alfalfa weevil model (degree days for peak occurrence of each stage, from R. I. Carruthers).

data.label: Aphid PVY vectors
data.notes: Estimates the typical risk of potato virus Y spread by winged aphids through the season, by degree days or calendar date, using curves fitted to Wisconsin's suction trap catches.

citations.text: Bradford, B. Z. and Groves, R. L. Aphid-vectored PVY risk by degree days from Wisconsin suction trap catches, 2016–2023. Vegetable Entomology Lab, UW–Madison, unpublished analysis (refitted 2026).

data.label: Black cutworm
data.notes: Times black cutworm egg laying, leaf feeding and the cutting stages from degree days after a significant moth capture, your trap date or May 1, so you know when to scout seedlings for cutting.

data.label: Cabbage maggot

data.notes: Times codling moth flight and egg hatch in apple orchards from degree days, from your first trap catch or one estimated for your latitude, and marks when to protect fruit during each generation's egg hatch.

data.notes: Follows Colorado potato beetle adults, egg masses and larvae through the season, by degree days or calendar date, using curves fitted to a decade of scouting counts in central Wisconsin's potato fields.

data.label: Corn earworm
data.notes: Times corn earworm caterpillars in sweet corn ears from degree days after egg laying, from the day you first find eggs on silks or catch a significant moth flight, or August 15 without a date.

data.label: Crucifer flea beetle
data.notes: Times crucifer flea beetle adults from degree days since January 1, the overwintered beetles that feed on seedlings and transplants in spring and the new adults of late summer, and marks when to scout new plantings every one to two days.
